strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: adapting critic-free, group-based advantage estimation (GRPO-style) to multi-agent LLM systems, where a shared critic over heterogeneous agent outputs is costly and unstable.

The method is described thoroughly: the two-phase rollout sampling + backward reward propagation procedure is formalized with equations, pseudo-code (Algorithms 1–5), agent-specific rewards, prompts, and hyperparameters, which supports reproducibility.
Three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) form a meaningful efficiency/effectiveness spectrum, and the paper honestly characterizes their trade-offs rather than only promoting one.

Experiments show consistent gains over MAPPO across three multi-hop QA datasets plus useful training-efficiency analysis (memory and time per step), and the paper includes a genuinely interesting analysis of why heterogeneous groups work (groups naturally becoming homogeneous during training, per-agent behavior evolution, format penalties, case study).
The 'no warm-up needed' observation and stability comparison against MAPPO address a practical pain point in MARL for LLMs.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is essentially applying GRPO-style relative advantages to a sequential LLM pipeline with different group-formation choices. Given existing multi-agent RL fine-tuning work (Chen et al. 2025 MARPO; Liao et al. 2025 MARFT), the claim of being the 'first systematic investigation of GOAs applied to MASs' needs stronger justification and closer positioning.

Missing critical baselines: there is no single-agent GRPO baseline that treats the whole pipeline trajectory as one sequence, no HAPPO or other critic-free MARL baseline, and no reproduction of Chen et al. (2025). Without these, it is hard to attribute gains to the heterogeneous-group mechanism specifically rather than to removing the critic in general.

Narrow evaluation scope: only one backbone (Llama3.1-8B), one linear three-agent topology, one training dataset (HotpotQA) for a single epoch, and single runs with no significance testing or seed variance. The claimed generalization to 'all MASs' is unsupported; the system is strictly a linear chain with no branching, loop, or heterogeneous-LLM setting.
Data hygiene concern: the validation set is defined as 'the first 500 samples from the test set', which conflates validation and test data and undermines the reported convergence analysis.

The theoretical grounding for heterogeneous-group advantage estimation (comparing responses to different prompts within a group) is weak; the paper offers only a post-hoc empirical explanation, and potential bias of cross-prompt advantage estimates is not analyzed.

Citation and presentation sloppiness: GRPO is attributed to 'Schulman et al. 2016' (that is GAE; GRPO is Shao et al. 2024/DeepSeekMath), Liao et al. appears twice as 2025a/2025b for the same paper, and several references are arXiv preprints with inconsistent venues.
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, which matters given the reliance on a specific verl-based implementation of multi-agent rollout.
Gains over MAPPO, while consistent, are moderate (roughly 2–4 F1 on in-domain HotpotQA, smaller elsewhere), and with one run each they may not be statistically robust.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: critic-free (GRPO-style) policy optimization for LLM-based multi-agent systems, with clear motivation for why critic-based MAPPO may be unstable and costly in heterogeneous-agent settings.

The method is described in reasonable detail: the two-phase rollout-and-backpropagation framework, heterogeneous group advantage estimation (Eq. 5), and three concrete sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are well specified, with full pseudocode (Algorithms 1–5), agent prompts, and reward design in the appendix, which supports reproducibility.

The empirical analysis goes beyond headline numbers: convergence curves, per-agent output pattern evolution (Fig. 8), intra-group similarity dynamics (Fig. 9), format-penalty traces, and a case study provide qualitative insight into why heterogeneous grouping works, and the memory/time comparison (Fig. 6) directly supports the efficiency claims.
Reported gains over MAPPO (Table 1) are consistent across the three variants and three QA datasets, and the 'no warm-up required' claim is an interesting and potentially useful practical finding.
The observation that heterogeneous groups naturally evolve into homogeneous ones during training is a genuinely interesting empirical finding that could inform future work on group-based MARL.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is essentially applying GRPO-style critic-free relative advantage estimation to a sequential MAS with parameter sharing and reward backpropagation. The paper's claim of being the 'first systematic investigation of GOAs applied to MASs' is overstated—Chen et al. (2025) and Liao et al. (2025a/b) already study RL for LLM-based MAS, and MHGPO is a relatively direct adaptation of existing single-agent techniques.

Theoretical soundness of heterogeneous grouping is unaddressed: computing relative advantages across rollouts generated from *different input prompts* (different sub-queries) conflates reward differences due to input difficulty with policy quality. The paper only offers a post-hoc empirical similarity argument (Fig. 9) rather than any analysis or justification of when this estimator is valid, or of its bias.

Narrow experimental scope: only one three-agent search system, one backbone (Llama3.1-8B), one group size (G=4), one training dataset (HotpotQA), and one epoch. The generalization claim in the conclusions ('capable of being generalized to general MAS') is asserted but not tested on any non-search MAS.

No statistical rigor: results are single-run (no seeds, no variance estimates, no significance tests), yet many claimed differences are small (e.g., RR vs. FoF on HotpotQA differ by ~0.4–0.5 points, and on MuSiQue MHGPO variants sometimes fall below MAPPO).

Model selection on test data: validation is performed on 'the first 500 samples from the test set' (Fig. 5), which constitutes direct test-set leakage for hyperparameter/strategy selection and undermines the test results in Table 1.

Missing baselines: only MAPPO is compared among MARL methods. Other relevant critic-free or multi-agent baselines (e.g., HAPPO, RLOO/REINFORCE-style variants, MARFT, or a simple token-level single-agent RL on the full trajectory) are absent, making it hard to attribute gains to the heterogeneous grouping specifically.

Citation errors and sloppiness: GRPO is attributed to 'Schulman et al. 2016' (the GAE paper), which is incorrect—GRPO originates with Shao et al. (2024). There are typos (e.g., 'stratgy'), figure 5 and figure 11 are largely redundant, and the 'Single LLM +RL' EM score of 0.500 in Table 1 is anomalous and unexplained.

The efficiency comparison (Fig. 6) is favorable partly because G is set to a very small value (4); the efficiency advantage over MAPPO likely shrinks or reverses at larger group sizes, and the paper does not explore the efficiency–performance trade-off across G.

The RR strategy's benefits depend on batch-level grouping of singleton rollouts with different inputs (Algorithm 5), which further weakens the semantic validity of the advantage estimate; the ablation between FoF and RR gains is thin and confounded by the probability hyperparameters (0.7, 0.1, 0.2), whose sensitivity is not studied.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending critic-free group-based optimization (GRPO/DAPO-style) to LLM-based multi-agent systems, addressing genuine limitations of critic-based MARL (instability, memory/compute overhead) in this setting.

The proposed heterogeneous group advantage estimation with backward reward propagation is a sensible and clearly described adaptation of GRPO to sequential multi-agent trajectories, and the paper is explicit about the key conceptual difference (rollouts within a group come from different prompts).

Three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are well designed, clearly illustrated (Figures 3-4), and specified in detail via algorithms in the appendix, giving a meaningful efficiency/effectiveness trade-off analysis.

Experiments include multiple multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue), efficiency measurements (GPU memory, wall-clock time), convergence curves, agent-behavior analyses (Figures 8-9), format-penalty analysis, and a case study, which together provide reasonable evidence for the claims about stability, faster convergence, and lower overhead relative to MAPPO.

The analysis of why heterogeneous groups work (parameter sharing + natural reduction of intra-group diversity over training, empirically supported by intra-group similarity measurements) is a thoughtful and somewhat convincing post-hoc explanation.

Reproducibility support is reasonably good: hyperparameter table, verl framework, hardware details, dataset statistics, full prompts, agent-specific rewards, and pseudocode for all sampling strategies are provided.
weaknesses: Narrow empirical scope: evaluation is limited to a single MAS architecture (linear 3-agent search pipeline) and a single backbone (Llama3.1-8B). Claims of generality to arbitrary MASs are stated but unvalidated, which weakens the central contribution.

Thin baseline coverage: MAPPO is the only MARL baseline. Obvious alternatives are missing, e.g., per-agent GRPO, DAPO, HAPPO, recent MAS-specific RL frameworks (MARFT, Chen et al. 2025-style setups), and an SFT warm-up comparison. The 'first systematic investigation of GOAs for MAS' claim is also vulnerable given rapidly emerging concurrent work.

Statistical rigor is limited: results appear to be from a single RL run per configuration with no random seeds, variance bands, or significance tests, despite the acknowledged training instability that motivates the work. Some margins over MAPPO are small, and on MuSiQue MHGPO-RR actually underperforms MAPPO, so 'consistently outperforms' is overstated.

Evaluation hygiene concern: the validation set is defined as 'the first 500 samples from the test set,' raising potential test-set contamination issues; proper train/dev/test splitting should be used.

The heterogeneous-group advantage estimator is biased (relative rewards computed over rollouts with different inputs), but no theoretical analysis of this bias or its conditions is provided; the justification rests on the empirical observation that groups homogenize over training, which is dataset/architecture dependent.

Backward reward propagation by simple averaging of successor rewards is a crude credit-assignment mechanism; no ablation of the aggregation operator or comparison against alternative credit assignment is provided.

Citation error: GRPO is attributed to 'Schulman et al. 2016' (the GAE paper) in the introduction; GRPO originates from DeepSeekMath (Shao et al. 2024, cited only as DeepSeek-R1 context). There is also a duplicated reference (Liao et al. 2025a/b).

Contribution novelty is incremental: the core idea is a relatively direct combination of GRPO with MAPPO's parameter-sharing paradigm plus rollout-grouping heuristics; the technical depth is modest and mainly empirical.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: extending critic-free group-based RL (GRPO-style) methods to multi-agent LLM search systems, where group rollouts span heterogeneous local contexts.

The proposed method is clearly described: backward reward propagation for indirect inter-agent dependencies plus heterogeneous-group advantage estimation, with three concrete rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) and an over-sampling variant, each with different efficiency–effectiveness trade-offs.

Empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive for the chosen setting: comparisons against MAPPO, PPO, GRPO, single-context RAG baselines (Search-o1, R1-Searcher), plus ablations on role-wise training, reward aggregation operators, reward sparsity, and group size, with multi-seed variance reported for several key tables.
Efficiency analysis (GPU memory, wall-clock time) substantiates the claim of a better performance–cost trade-off than critic-based MAPPO, which is a practically meaningful contribution.

The appendix offers a careful conceptual analysis connecting MHGPO to single-context GRPO under explicit assumptions (A1–A3), with honest discussion of what the equivalence does and does not establish.

The limitations section is candid and accurate (QA-only scope, 8B scale, fixed 3-agent topology, missing variance analysis), and the discussion of progressive homogenization vs. entropy collapse is appropriately hedged rather than overclaimed.
weaknesses: Narrow empirical scope relative to the general claims: all experiments use one fixed three-agent linear pipeline (Rewriter→Reranker→Answerer), one backbone (Llama3.1-8B), and training on HotpotQA only. The claim that the framework applies to arbitrary n-agent MASs is asserted but never tested, so the contribution is really an empirical finding for one system family.

Key comparisons lack statistical rigor: Table 1 (the main results) reports no variance over seeds, and gains of MHGPO variants over MAPPO, especially out-of-domain, are sometimes small (e.g., RR vs. MAPPO on MuSiQue). The significance of headline improvements is therefore hard to assess.

The 'first systematic study of GOAs for MASS' claim is somewhat overstated: closely related concurrent/preceding work on multi-agent RL fine-tuning for LLMs (e.g., MARFT, Chen et al. 2025b using MAPPO for multi-agent RAG) exists, and the delta relative to simply applying GRPO on a single-context transcript (as in R1-Searcher) is analyzed only indirectly and conceptually rather than with a directly matched baseline.

The theoretical connection (Appendix D) rests on the strong context-sufficiency assumption (A3), which the authors themselves admit rarely holds in practice; the analysis is a conceptual bridge, and no variance or convergence analysis of heterogeneous grouping is provided, leaving the central mechanism (why heterogeneous groups beat homogeneous ones beyond the IS ablation) empirically but not theoretically grounded.

Potential bias in the RR strategy is not analyzed: regrouping singleton rollouts across different root questions (Algorithm 3) mixes unrelated inputs into one advantage-normalization group, and the paper does not quantify or justify this beyond the empirical result.

Concerns about entropy collapse are acknowledged but left unresolved; the reported homogenization trend could equally indicate reduced exploration, and only short-horizon (one-epoch) training is examined.

No explicit statement about code or artifact release, which limits reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables; some implementation details (e.g., retrieval corpus construction, contriever index) would still require substantial effort to replicate.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: extending critic-free, group-based RL (GRPO-style) from single-context reasoning to multi-agent search systems, where cross-trajectory normalization over heterogeneous groups is a sensible mechanism for credit assignment and global system-level optimization.

The method is clearly and formally specified: backward reward propagation (Eq. 4), heterogeneous-group advantage estimation (Eq. 5), and the full objective (Eq. 6) are well-defined, and the three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are concretely described with complete pseudocode in the appendix.

The experimental section is broad in coverage: training dynamics, resource/memory profiling, OOD evaluation on 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue, ablations over agent roles, aggregation operators, group sizes, reward sparsity, plus a case study — this goes beyond a bare main-results table.

The theoretical appendix (single-context transcript equivalence under A1–A3) is honestly framed as a conceptual bridge rather than an overclaimed result, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges QA-only scope, 8B scale, fixed 3-agent topology, and missing variance analysis.
Reproducibility materials are relatively good: hyperparameter table, prompts, reward design, hardware, dataset details, and algorithms are provided.
weaknesses: Limited external validation against the relevant competing literature: the only MARL-for-MAS baseline is MAPPO. No comparison with HAPPO, MA-RFT/MARFT (cited as related), or closely concurrent critic-free multi-agent group-RL methods (e.g., GiGPO-style hierarchical group advantage), so the claim of being the 'first systematic study of GOAs for MASS' and of superior performance is hard to verify — the marginal contribution over Chen et al. (2025b)'s MAPPO-on-multi-agent-RAG pipeline is not sharply delineated.

The main results table (Table 1) lacks standard deviations and appears to be single-run, while the paper itself shows seed variance of ±0.2–0.8 in ablations; several headline gaps (e.g., MHGPO-FoF vs. RR vs. FoF(os)) are small relative to plausible run-to-run noise, weakening the claimed 'consistently outperforms' conclusions.

The evidence base is narrow for the generality implied: one linear 3-agent pipeline, one backbone (Llama3.1-8B), a single training dataset (HotpotQA) for all OOD claims, one epoch of training, and a small G; the authors acknowledge these, but they collectively constrain the supported contribution to this specific MASS instance.

The core theoretical result rests on a strong context-sufficiency assumption (A3) whose practical satisfaction is asserted rather than verified for the actual prompts; the 'near-aligned per-token advantage' claim in the contributions is thus weaker than it first appears, and no variance analysis of heterogeneous grouping is provided despite the method explicitly adding reward variance.

Some analysis is post-hoc and not fully convincing: the 'progressive homogenization' explanation for why heterogeneous grouping works is descriptive, the entropy-collapse concern is acknowledged but unresolved, and the IS baseline's underperformance conflates several design choices (sample budget, group formation, agent independence), making the causal attribution of gains to heterogeneity less clean than claimed.
No code release is mentioned, which, combined with the complexity of the rollout/grouping machinery and single-run main results, hampers reproducibility of the headline claims.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: extending critic-free group-based optimization (GRPO) to multi-agent, multi-context search systems, addressing a real limitation of MAPPO-style methods (critic instability, memory/compute overhead).

The paper is systematic: it introduces a general framework (backward reward propagation + heterogeneous-group advantage estimation) and carefully studies three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) plus an over-sampling variant, with an explicit analysis of sample-efficiency vs. optimization-quality trade-offs.

Empirical evidence is reasonably comprehensive: main results on three multi-hop QA benchmarks (in-domain and OOD), comparison against PPO/GRPO, MAPPO, single-context RAG systems (Search-o1, R1-Searcher), efficiency measurements (GPU memory, wall-clock time), and multiple targeted ablations (role-wise training, aggregation operator, composite vs. final-only reward, group size), some with error bars over three seeds.

The analysis of *why* heterogeneous grouping works (Section 4.3, Appendix C.3) goes beyond raw numbers, including intra-group similarity trends and an honest discussion of entropy-collapse concerns; Figure 7 behavior traces and the case study add qualitative insight.

The theoretical appendix is a genuine strength: it formalizes the relationship between MHGPO and single-context GRPO via explicit assumptions (A1–A3), with propositions and proofs for score-function and GRPO-style gradients, and is candid that the equivalence is a conceptual anchor rather than an implementation claim.

Reproducibility support is above average for this area: full algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, agent prompts, reward specifications, and hardware details are provided; the Limitations section is unusually candid (QA-only, 8B scale, fixed 3-agent pipeline, incomplete theory).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat undercut by the paper's own theory: under assumptions A1–A3, MHGPO reduces exactly to GRPO applied to a single-context tool-augmented transcript (akin to agentic traces in R1-Searcher). The practical gains therefore hinge on the relaxed-A3 regime and heterogeneous grouping, whose advantage estimates are provably not unbiased for the per-agent policy (a downstream agent conditioned on a poor upstream prefix receives low reward regardless of its own action). The paper acknowledges this but offers no variance/stability analysis, so the central methodological claim rests largely on empirical results.

External validity is narrow: a single backbone (Llama3.1-8B), a single fixed 3-agent linear pipeline, training on HotpotQA only for one epoch, and QA-only rewards (F1 + format penalties). The claim that the framework generalizes to broader MASs is asserted but untested; results with larger teams or non-linear topologies would substantially strengthen the contribution.

Some experimental reporting is inconsistent: it is unclear whether the main Table 1 results are averaged over multiple seeds (error bars appear only in ablation tables), the definition of 'Accuracy' as token-level prediction accuracy is non-standard, and Figure 6 cost measurements are averaged over only the first 50 steps of training.

The 'first systematic study of GOAs for MASS' claim is difficult to verify given concurrent work (e.g., MARFT, multi-agent RAG RL of Chen et al. 2025b) and should be softened or more carefully positioned.
No explicit code release is stated, which, combined with the complexity of the rollout/grouping machinery (fork_on, RR regrouping), limits reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

Gains over the strongest baseline (R1-Searcher variants and MAPPO) are meaningful but modest on some metrics and datasets, and the MHGPO variant ordering is not uniformly consistent across datasets (e.g., RR vs. FoF(os) on OOD), suggesting sensitivity to the sampling strategy choice that the paper does not fully explain.
